#10544. AI data centers also lost big in the 2026 midterm elections

President Donald Trump wasn’t on the ballot this midterm election season, but on some tickets, an industry he wholeheartedly supports was: Ballot measures in more than 30 districts across the country asked voters to weigh in on AI data center development.

And data centers lost big. 

Voters overwhelmingly chose to ban or pause local data center development across 38 out of 41 ballot measures. (The other three measures aren’t yet reporting results, according to Ballotpedia.)

The ballot questions varied, in some instances asking voters to prohibit data centers in their cities, and in others, asking them to allow data center development, or even to uphold specific data center deals. 

Where were data centers on the ballot?

Not all results are yet in. But it’s still clear that no matter the framing, data centers lost by landslides.

In Edgewater, Florida, more than 77% of voters approved a ballot initiative to amend the city charter in order to “prohibit the approval, construction, expansion, or operation of new data centers.” 

In Ashville, Ohio, a ballot referendum asked voters to maintain the village’s deal with EdgeConneX for two data centers and on-site natural gas across nearly 200 acres. Residents struck it down with more than 81% of the vote. 

Grove City, Ohio, saw one of the closest races, but it’s still looking bad for data centers. It looks like voters there still chose to rein in data center development—by requiring public approval for certain projects—with 55% of the vote. 

In 28 of the 38 ballot measures for which Ballotpedia is reporting results, support for banning or pausing data center development hit 70% or more. In 13, it hit 80% or more. 

Strong support for data center critics

Data centers didn’t only lose when it came to specific ballot questions, either. Candidates who spoke out against data centers won handily.

In some cases, candidates seemed to sense the public rebuke of data centers early on, and switched their tune.

Democrat Pennsylvania Governor Josh Shapiro, for example, was once in support of the AI data center boom. Then in August he signed an executive order to restrict certain projects and require them to be approved by local officials. 

“We will not be bulldozed by the lawyers working for these big tech companies,” he said at the time, according to NBC News. He won a second term on Tuesday. 

In Georgia, Democrat Keisha Lance Bottoms, who won her race for governor, made a statewide data center pause a key part of her campaign. Georgia is one of the leading states for data center development.

Texas, too, is a major data center hub, with more than 781 data centers either operating, under construction, or planned across nearly 300 campuses, according to Cleanview. 

Outgoing Texas Governor Greg Abbott, who lost his reelection bid, did recently introduce a data center moratorium, but he had backed the industry before, and even raised about $9 million from data center donors. 

Governor-elect Democrat Gina Hinojosa, Abbott’s opponent, called that temporary moratorium a “scam.” She campaigned on data center opposition, promising a new construction moratorium, an end to data center tax breaks, and tighter regulations around water and power use. 

Across both parties, midterm campaigns and outside groups spent more than $173 million in anti-data center ad spending. Democrats led that charge, with $140 million of that spending, versus Republicans with $28 million. 

The data center industry fought back, setting up a super PAC that set aside $1.5 million in ads to supporting Republican Darline Graham, who was fighting to keep her late brother Lindsey Graham’s Senate seat in South Carolina.

She lost to Democrat Annie Andrews in what New York Times reporter Teddy Schleifer called “a black eye for the data-center industry.”

Trump has gone all-in on data centers and AI companies, even writing “let Data Reign” on Truth Social in August. Voters clearly disagree.

#10541. Jeff Bezos praised Raising Cane’s. Its founder built a $22 billion fortune by breaking 3 fast-food rules

Raising Cane’s isn’t following the standard fast-food playbook.

From its limited menu to the employee dress code, founder Todd Graves is charting his own path in a competitive industry. Now, one of the world’s richest men is pointing to his chicken finger empire as a prime example of the power of entrepreneurship.

In a recent Fox News interview, Jeff Bezos pushed back on the notion that building a successful business and becoming a billionaire made someone a villain.

Instead, he pointed to entrepreneurs who expanded their companies and created thousands of jobs. For the Amazon founder, Graves is a prime example of that.

“There’s nothing wrong with making unbelievably good chicken that people love,” he said. “And it doesn’t make him a bad person.”

However, although Graves and Bezos are both billionaires, the former followed a different playbook than the latter.

In 1996, Graves, who was 24, opened the first Raising Cane’s in Baton Rouge, Louisiana. He used loans from friends, family, and the Small Business Administration, as well as savings from his jobs as a boilermaker and an Alaskan salmon fisherman.

Three decades later, the ethos of the fast-food chain remains the same: a simple menu centered on chicken fingers, fries, coleslaw, Texas toast, and Cane’s Sauce.

Even now, the smallest change, such as the addition of a sandwich combo, can create anxiety and stress.

“To tell you the truth, man, I kind of wish we didn’t even have it on the menu. It’s like 3 or 4 percent of sales. And it slows us down,” Graves previously told Inc. “I wish we didn’t have it, but I won’t take it away now.”

This small admission reflects the chicken chain’s broader philosophy. While Bezos launched a publicly traded giant, Graves has focused on keeping Raising Cane’s limited in scope and tightly controlled.

Keeping the company private

The biggest difference between the two billionaires may be their views on taking a company public.

Forbes estimates Graves currently owns about 92 percent of the company, with a net worth of approximately $22 billion. The founder has said Raising Cane’s has no plans to go public, a choice he has tied to preserving the chain’s culture.

A key executive has echoed the same sentiment. “We have no plans on that,” AJ Kumaran, the company’s co-CEO and COO, told Restaurant Business. “We are privately held because we want to remain that way.”

By comparison, Bezos took Amazon public just three years after its founding. It debuted on the stock market in May 1997 at $18 a share, raising $54 million to fuel its growth.

Focusing on employees

However, even though Graves is committed to retaining control of the business, he takes a more relaxed approach with his employees.

At Raising Cane’s, crew members wear casual uniforms and music has been allowed in the kitchen since the early days. It is a deliberately relaxed approach that stands apart from Amazon’s more regimented structure.

A commitment to charity

Yet, even amid their differing approaches to business, both Bezos and Graves are committed to charitable giving.

Bezos’s Earth Fund, backed by a $10 billion pledge, has distributed about $2.4 billion to date. His Day 1 Families Fund has donated more than $850 million to nonprofits addressing homelessness.

After the Texas floods in 2025, Graves donated $1 million to the Red Cross. In August, Graves told Dallas Weekly that the company had given more than $165 million to charitable causes over its first 30 years, something he hopes will continue.

Raising Cane’s didn’t immediately respond to a request from Inc. for comment.

—Amaya Nichole

This article originally appeared on Fast Company’s sister website, Inc.com.

#10538. CVS is splitting into 2 companies: Healthcare giant’s ‘Pharmacy’ breakup explained

CVS is breaking up.

On Wednesday, the healthcare giant announced plans to split into two separate, independent companies, and both will be publicly traded. 

The two companies will form a “leading healthcare solutions company” called CVS Health, and will encompass Aetna, CVS Caremark, CVS Specialty, Oak Street Health, and Signify Health.

The second company, dubbed CVS Pharmacy, will be made up of roughly 9,000 CVS pharmacies, mail pharmacy, MinuteClinic, and the Health100 tech services business.

The company also announced that current CVS Health chair and CEO David Joyner will serve as CEO of the “new” CVS Health, and Prem Shah, current Group President of CVS Health, will be the CEO of the “new” CVS Pharmacy.

“Our history is defined by proactively evolving to stay ahead of what’s next in healthcare, and in today’s environment, that means delivering more affordability, greater access, and a simpler experience,” said Joyner in a statement. “From a position of strength, and a focus on the long term, we plan to create two focused companies to improve consumer engagement, affordability, and care coordination.”

CVS shares were down approximately 12% on Wednesday morning.

As for the reason for the split?

Notably, the move effectively reverses, in some respects, the 2018 merger between CVS Health and Aetna.

According to company leadership, two smaller companies would be able to be more efficient and nimble than one single, larger one. When the dust settles, CVS Pharmacy will basically be a pharmacy company, while CVS Health will be focused on insurance and other services.

Regulatory concerns may also be at play. For example, The New York Times reports that some states, such as Arkansas and Tennessee, have passed laws in recent years that prevent large conglomerates from managing prescription benefits while simultaneously running retail and mail-order pharmacy services. 

Other companies have taken on similar strategies in recent years. Notably, Comcast is breaking off its media and technology businesses, it announced earlier this year, which likewise follows NBCUniversal’s decision to spin off some of its brands into another company, Versant.

Further, Madison Square Garden Sports is spinning off its pro sports franchises (the NHL’s New York Rangers and the NBA’s New York Knicks) into separate companies. And Keurig Dr Pepper recently announced plans to spin off its coffee division.

A new website seeks to distill over 10,000 public comments across more than 410 local governments, and it's bad news for data center builders.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

As more and more AI data centers are being built across the United States, the backlash is starting to gather pace. Following the recent news that Amazon canceled plans to build four new facilities after a public outcry, a new website seeks to detail how sour public sentiment on the subject has turned. American Sentiment is operated by Prophecy Gov, an AI startup based in San Francisco, and it has turned 10,202 public comments at 417 local government meetings from 2026 into a scrollable collection of facts and figures that will give data center builders nightmares, revealing that more than 90% of public comments on data centers are negative.

The website notes that, while public comments don't always match the country's true sentiment, it's clear that the discussion around data center buildouts has reached a "fever pitch" of late. That's something borne out by the data, which takes in 48 states and 417 local governments, with 906 public meetings tracked. Of the 10,202 comments, 90.5% were negative, with just 7% saying positive things about the potential for a new data center being built in their backyard. The remaining 2.5% simply asked questions about the subject. A staggering 73% of meetings had no data center supporters whatsoever. Even those who did support the prospect of a data center being built found themselves outnumbered 6:1, according to the stats.

Predictably, a range of concerns were raised in opposition to data centers, with water use being the most common. In May this year, it was reported that a single AI data center project had consumed 29 million gallons of water. It used so much water, in fact, that local residents noticed a drop in water pressure as a result. A month later, Microsoft claimed its new AI data centers use as little water annually as a restaurant. Beyond water consumption, the impact on local quality of life and the lack of transparency around the project made up the top three complaints. These concerns aren't offset by the benefits of building such facilities, with many people saying that they didn't believe that the claimed benefits would ever come to fruition. Perhaps surprisingly, AI and its potential negative effects weren't mentioned in 4/5 of the comments. Just 21% made any mention of AI as a whole.

Members of the public called out some of AI's biggest players when arguing against data centers, including Google, Amazon, Meta, and Microsoft. Concerns also turned personal, with SpaceX/xAI CEO Elon Musk by far the most mentioned during meetings, followed by OpenAI CEO Sam Altman. Notably, Palantir's Peter Thiel was third, ahead of Meta's Mark Zuckerberg and Jeff Bezos when discussing Amazon.

At a time when the United States may seem more divided than ever, the lack of desire for local data centers appears to be a thoroughly bipartisan issue. Red and blue counties oppose the prospect at almost exactly the same rate, although rural counties raised different issues than urban and suburban ones. The former most commonly worried about the impact on a community's character, farmland, and property rights. Commenters in urban and suburban areas raised the issues of transparency, government distrust, air pollution, and utility bills more often. Pollution is one issue that has been raised previously — a report earlier this month warned that U.S. data centers could wipe out 15 years of progress in greenhouse gas emissions.

There was one group of people largely in favor of new data centers, however. 79% of commenters who said they were union workers were in favor of data centers. Conversely, just 3% of property owners and 3% of residents agreed. Even just 40% of data center workers were in favor of actual data centers, according to the figures.

#10535. How AI impacts solopreneurs’ relationships with their clients (and what to do about it)

Most people I know have asked themselves some version of “Is AI replacing me?” It’s a fair question. 

But, running a solo business, I think the question extends beyond “Is AI replacing the work I do?” It’s also impacted the way clients interact with the people they hire. 

Clients expect AI to make your work cheaper

Some companies are really moving their budgets away from hiring people to AI. The Ramp Economics Lab tracked how businesses split their spending between freelance marketplaces and AI model providers. Among the companies it studied, the share of spend going to freelance marketplaces dropped from 0.66% in the fourth quarter of 2021 to 0.14% in the third quarter of 2025. Over the same time period, the share going to AI model providers climbed from zero to nearly 3%.

How far that shift goes varies from company to company and the type of service provided. But clients know AI is cheaper (Ramp’s data bears that out). As a result, some clients may expect to pay less for human work. I suspect this is because they think that if AI allows the solopreneur to work faster, then they, the client, should get some benefit. 

I don’t think solopreneurs should drop their rates to compete with AI, because that devalues the end result that the client is paying for. If a client’s budget has shrunk, you might cut the scope before you reduce your rates. You could also offer more flexible terms, like ad hoc or on-demand work, so a client with a tight budget can still bring you in when they need you.

When a client runs your work through AI

Clients now have a free “second opinion” on everything you deliver. They can paste your work into a chatbot and ask for a critique, and the answer will sound confident (even if it’s confidently wrong). AI feedback also tends to be generic. It can misunderstand the project’s goals or what the client hired you for—forcing you to respond to a robot’s assessment.

It helps to cover AI upfront, either during a discovery call or in the contract. You might explain how you use AI yourself and how you respond to requests for changes to the deliverables.

I know some solopreneurs who let clients know that they won’t consider AI-generated feedback, like a long email that was clearly written by AI. Whether or not you go that far, the scope of the project should clearly limit how much feedback gets incorporated into any revisions you make.

Getting found when everyone’s outreach sounds like AI

Cold pitches and social posts are now full of AI-generated content, so the usual ways of finding clients don’t work as well.

I’m on the receiving end of many cold pitches, and my inbox is now flooded with emails written by AI. I also used to find clients for my business through LinkedIn, but it feels impossible at times to stand out among the “noise.”

These days, personal connections reign supreme. It feels like the only surefire way to make sure you break through the AI content: having people who know you, understand what you do, can vouch for your work, and are willing to refer you.

The effort it takes to connect with people on a human level also goes further when so much of the outreach around you sounds like it came from the same template.

The clients worth keeping want a human collaborator

The people and companies trying to replace work with AI aren’t necessarily a fit for you anyway. They don’t value the human aspect of that particular type of work, and you’re not going to convince them otherwise. It might mean the pool of potential clients is smaller, in addition to a more challenging environment to find clients in the first place. Put it all together, and it’s a stressful time to run a business.

But if you can find the right clients, they’ll appreciate you more. My own clients hire me for judgment and expertise, and they still want a person behind that work.

#10534. Samsung’s advanced sleep apnea detection is coming to these Galaxy wearables

Samsung announced a new, advanced version of its AI-powered sleep apnea detection, and which devices it will appear on in November.

Sleep apnea detection was first introduced to Galaxy devices in 2024, after Samsung gained approval from the FDA in the US. The tool was offered as a baseline detection feature, so users who might be suffering from frequent breathing interruptions during sleep would be aware and seek further medical help.

Samsung says its new and improved version uses an AI algorithm to analyze breathing disturbances per hour (via GSMArena). It goes beyond detection and breaks those disturbances down into more granular detail – closer to something a dedicated sleep study would be equipped to do.

Users will need to record at least five hours of sleep twice within 10 days for the sleep apnea detection tool to properly get results on their Galaxy Watch or Ring.

Samsung is still adamant that this tool does not replace professional diagnosis; it’s simply better at making the user aware of their sleep habits.

Selling the exact same model worldwide at the same price while disabling features under the guise of country restriction is unfair. For example, keeping health features inactive in certain regions under the name of FDA approval. If Samsung wanted to, they could easily enable features like blood pressure and ECG for non-medical use for Bangladesh—or at least in countries where these features aren't legally prohibited—for health awareness. Not doing so feels like a form of deception toward customers.

Samsung says the new sleep apnea detection feature will roll out in November, starting in Korea, after the tool was approved by the Ministry of Food and Drug Safety. It’s FDA-approved in the US, as well, so it should follow shortly.

So far, Samsung has detailed these wearables:

After the initial rollout, the Galaxy Watch 7 and Watch 8 will get an update as long as they’re running Wear OS 7.0 or later.

There are no plans to dismantle the current sleep apnea detection tool available on the Galaxy Watch 4 and later.

#10531. Building CRM Automations That Don't Break: APIs, Webhooks, and AI Validation

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Have 30-200 Employees? Make $50k-$500k selling your data for AI Training.

Stay up to date with AI tools, model releases, and developer workflows that matter.

Modern businesses rarely struggle with a shortage of software. The bigger problem is getting their existing systems to communicate properly.

A lead arrives through a website form, but the sales team doesn't receive a notification. Someone books an appointment, yet their CRM record isn't updated. A prospect replies to an automated message, but the follow-up sequence continues as though nothing happened.

These are integration problems rather than software problems.

Platforms such as GoHighLevel aim to solve them by combining contact management, messaging, appointment scheduling and workflow automation in one environment. However, the real value comes from how these components are configured and connected to other applications.

For developers, agencies and technical consultants, GoHighLevel provides an interesting example of how low-code automation and API-driven development can work together.

This guide explores the architecture behind an effective CRM automation system, how GoHighLevel's integrations operate, and where custom development makes sense. The patterns below — data normalisation, idempotent event handling, queue-based processing and validated AI outputs — apply to any CRM; GoHighLevel is used here as the running example because it combines native workflows with a public API and webhooks in one platform.

It's tempting to think of automation as a collection of simple rules.

When someone submits a form, send an email. When a customer books a meeting, update their status. When a payment arrives, trigger a notification.

Individually, these are straightforward tasks.

Problems emerge when different workflows start interacting.

Consider a business that generates leads through several channels:

Referral partners and external lead providers

Each channel introduces different information, sometimes in different formats.

One source might supply a full name, phone number and email address. Another provides only a phone number. A third might include campaign information, product preferences or qualification answers.

Without a consistent data structure, CRM records become fragmented. Duplicate contacts appear, important information disappears and automations begin acting on incomplete data.

A well-designed system needs to address these problems before adding more workflow complexity.

GoHighLevel combines native workflow tools with an API that allows developers to integrate external services.

Its core components include contact records, conversations, calendars, opportunities, pipelines and workflow automation.

Developers can interact with supported resources through the platform's REST API, while webhooks provide a mechanism for reacting to events.

Information enters the system through forms, funnels, integrations, inbound communication or API requests.

At this stage, the priority is collecting reliable information and associating it with the correct contact.

Once information has been received, workflows can evaluate conditions and initiate actions.

For example, a newly created lead might trigger an internal notification, a qualification sequence or an appointment invitation.

Some business processes require functionality beyond the CRM's native capabilities.

An organisation might need to synchronise an accounting platform, update an external database or pass information into a proprietary application.

This is where APIs, webhooks and middleware become especially useful.

The important architectural decision is determining which tasks belong inside the CRM and which should be handled externally.

GoHighLevel's developer platform offers REST endpoints for supported operations involving contacts, conversations, calendars, payments and other CRM resources.

Its API uses JSON and supports token-based authentication, including OAuth 2.0 for applications requiring delegated access.

For developers creating an internal integration, a Private Integration Token may be appropriate. Public applications serving multiple accounts generally require a different authentication architecture.

A basic API request follows a familiar pattern:

This example illustrates the structure of a contact-creation request. Production implementations should validate the current endpoint schema, manage tokens securely, handle retries and consider using an upsert operation when duplicate prevention is required.

Two production details deserve attention up front. First, treat a 429 rate-limit response as a normal control signal, not an error: back off exponentially, respect any retry-after value, and never retry in a tight loop. Second, prefer upserts keyed on a stable identifier (a normalised phone number or email address) over blind creates, so a retried request cannot spawn a duplicate contact.

The same principles apply when synchronising information from external applications.

For example, an insurance business might receive enquiries through a specialist quoting system. Rather than manually transferring those records, an integration could normalise the information and send it to the CRM.

The key is to treat the API as part of a broader data architecture, not merely as another way to trigger messages.

APIs are useful when an application needs to retrieve or modify information.

Webhooks address a different requirement: knowing when something has happened.

A webhook-driven architecture might look like this:

A configured webhook sends event data to an external endpoint.

The receiving application verifies and processes the event.

This is particularly useful when connecting CRM activity to internal dashboards, fulfilment systems or custom databases.

However, webhook integrations require careful handling.

A publicly accessible webhook endpoint shouldn't automatically trust every request it receives.

Where the platform provides signature verification, developers should validate the signature using the documented method before processing the payload. In practice this means computing an HMAC over the raw request body with the shared signing secret and comparing it to the signature header in constant time — never parsing the body first and re-serialising it, which can change the bytes the signature was computed over.

If an appointment event triggers an invoice, processing the same event twice could create duplicate invoices.

An idempotent handler should recognise an event that has already been processed and avoid repeating side effects. The reliable way to do this is to store each event's unique ID (or a hash of its payload) in a small processed-events table and check it before running any side effect — a duplicate delivery then becomes a cheap no-op instead of a second invoice.

Long-running operations shouldn't necessarily execute inside the initial webhook request.

A more resilient approach is to validate the event, record it, acknowledge receipt and place any substantial work on a processing queue. Return a 2xx response within a second or two so the sender does not retry, then let a worker handle the slow steps. Failed jobs should retry with exponential backoff and, after a set number of attempts, land in a dead-letter queue where a human can inspect them instead of being retried forever.

This helps prevent slow third-party services from disrupting event handling.

Consider a company receiving enquiries through paid advertising, website forms and telephone calls.

The objective is simple: respond quickly, qualify potential customers and book appointments.

A practical CRM workflow could follow several stages.

Incoming data should be converted into a consistent format.

Phone numbers should be standardised, source information should be preserved, and duplicate detection should be considered before creating another contact.

It's also important to retain communication preferences and the relevant consent information.

Not every lead should be distributed randomly.

Assignment logic might consider geographical territory, product category, team availability or an existing customer relationship.

For more complicated organisations, routing decisions may need to be calculated in an external service.

Once the lead has been assigned, the system can initiate an appropriate follow-up.

This might involve notifying a sales representative, sending a permitted acknowledgement or offering an appointment booking link.

The workflow needs to respond to changing circumstances.

If the prospect books an appointment, unnecessary booking reminders should stop.

If a sales representative takes ownership, automated outreach may need to pause.

If the prospect opts out, the system must respect that preference across relevant communication channels.

Finally, the system should record what happened.

Useful measurements include lead response time, appointment booking rate, appointment attendance and conversion rate.

These metrics make it possible to distinguish a workflow that simply runs from one that improves business operations.

Artificial intelligence introduces additional possibilities, particularly around lead qualification, conversation handling and information extraction.

An AI-powered system might analyse an incoming enquiry, identify the customer's requirements and suggest an appropriate next action.

It could also summarise a conversation for a sales representative or help classify enquiries into different service categories.

However, introducing an AI model creates new engineering considerations.

Allowing an AI model to generate unrestricted text is rarely sufficient when that output controls business processes.

A more predictable approach is to require structured responses and validate them before updating CRM records.

The application should check that the response matches the expected schema before performing any action.

Some actions are better handled by deterministic rules.

Communication consent, payment processing, account permissions and important customer record changes shouldn't depend solely on a language model's interpretation.

AI can help classify or summarise information, but critical operations should remain subject to validated rules and appropriate human oversight.

AI assistants can reduce repetitive work, but they should also recognise their limitations.

A prospect asking an unusual technical question or requesting a customised proposal may need to speak with a person.

The best automation systems provide clear escalation paths rather than trying to automate every possible interaction.

GoHighLevel's visual workflow builder makes many routine automations accessible to non-developers.

A basic appointment reminder or lead notification may require little custom development.

The situation changes when several systems need to work together.

For example, a business might need to migrate thousands of existing contacts, integrate custom booking software, synchronise records with an accounting platform and implement specialised lead routing.

These projects require more than familiarity with a visual workflow editor.

They involve data modelling, integration architecture, testing, security and operational reliability.

The decision rule is straightforward: use native workflows for anything the platform already does well, and write custom code only where the platform's model runs out — multi-source routing, external system synchronisation, or reporting that spans several platforms. That distinction matters because unnecessary custom development can make a system harder to maintain, while forcing every process into native workflows can create an equally fragile architecture.

Even technically capable teams can run into problems when implementing CRM integrations.

Large workflows containing dozens of branches are difficult to test and maintain.

Smaller, clearly defined workflows are generally easier to troubleshoot.

An integration that works with ten contacts may behave very differently when processing thousands of records.

Developers should account for rate limits, batch processing, exponential backoff and retry behaviour.

Creating a new contact for every incoming event can quickly damage CRM data quality.

Contact matching, normalisation and carefully selected identifiers help reduce duplication.

Access tokens should never be exposed in client-side JavaScript or committed to public repositories.

Use appropriate secret management and grant integrations only the permissions they require.

Successful execution doesn't necessarily mean the system behaves correctly.

Test scenarios should cover missing information, duplicate events, failed API requests, appointment cancellations, opt-outs and unexpected responses from external services.

Observability matters too. Logs and alerts should help identify which step failed and whether the operation can be retried safely.

Not every automation problem needs an API integration.

A useful decision framework is to start with the simplest reliable implementation.

Standard appointment reminders — Native CRM workflows

Basic lead assignment — Native workflows where supported

External application synchronisation — API or integration middleware

Complex routing across several data sources — Custom logic with CRM integration

AI-assisted lead classification — AI service with validated outputs

Enterprise reporting across multiple platforms — Dedicated reporting or data pipeline

Hybrid architectures are often the most practical.

The CRM manages customer interactions and standard business processes, while specialised services handle requirements that benefit from custom code.

This separation can also make future maintenance more manageable.

CRM automation has become considerably more accessible, but ease of implementation shouldn't be confused with reliability.

A workflow that sends a message after a form submission is easy to demonstrate. A system that handles thousands of contacts, prevents duplication, respects communication preferences, synchronises multiple applications and recovers gracefully from failures requires more careful design.

GoHighLevel provides a useful foundation for combining customer management with automation, particularly when its native capabilities are supported by well-designed integrations.

For developers, the opportunity isn't simply to automate more tasks. It's to design systems that remain understandable, maintainable and reliable as businesses grow.

The strongest implementations aren't necessarily the ones with the most workflows, API connections or AI features.

They're the ones where the right information reaches the right system at the right time — and everything continues working when something inevitably goes wrong.

The 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 launched at a price of $120 in January 2025.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Raspberry Pi boss Eben Upton has officially announced price rises for some 16GB products. Specifically, the price of the 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 is being raised by $80 to $385, and the 16GB Raspberry Pi Compute Module 5 will go up by $40. In a glimmer of better news, the price of the Raspberry Pi 500+ all-in-one desktop, which also features a 16GB model, is being held, but it was already rather pricey.

Upton framed the decision to raise prices as being due to “the steep rises in the cost of memory over the past two years.” He explained that other computer makers have had to make similar decisions recently. That sounds fair, and he added that Raspberry Pi had been doing what they could to minimize costs passed on to customers.

The price rise of the headline 16GB Raspberry Pi 5 to $385 is effective immediately. As is the $40 increase to the CM5 16GB variant. Of course, both these 16GB devices have seen prior increases in price since being launched at $120 and $135, respectively.

Some moderately good news was that there would be no price increase today for the Raspberry Pi 500+ 16GB all-in-one keyboard wedge computer. Upton didn’t mention that this is already rather expensive at $485, though.

Indeed, there have been several waves of price increases affecting Pis since the components RAMpocalypse began. Only a month ago we saw a similar cost-of-memory post by Upton on the official blog, this time accompanied by news that there were price increases being implemented for the 2GB Raspberry Pi 4 and Raspberry Pi 5 models. Prices of both rose by $12.50, to $67.50 and $77.50, respectively. Perhaps this price gulf between the 2GB and 16GB Pi 5 helps highlight the heavy impact of RAM pricing even more clearly than today’s blog. 1GB devices haven’t seen price rises recently.

The price rises, and comparison in prices between high-and-low memory density models makes it all the more important “to make sure you’re not paying for more memory than you need,” indicates the Raspberry Pi blog about the latest price increases. Sadly for the Pi business, hobbyists and makers already seem to be moving away from the full-sized Pi and CM products for many DIY projects.

Higher pricing is affecting all sorts of computer products, but it might have a particular impact on Raspberry Pi’s business. Generations of this device were explicitly designed around a strict budget constraint, and very famously stuck to a $25–$35 target price for many years.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

Now the core Raspberry Pi business is being squeezed by simpler microcontrollers at the low end, where the use of Picos and ESP32 boards have become increasingly popular for small projects. At the other end of the market, with some Pis approaching $400 or $500, makers start to eye entry-level x86 SBCs and mini PCs. Even a cheap mini PC can be powerful with a stronger CPU, GPU, NPU, and more. Mini PCs can win on flexibility and expandability too, and there’s a wide variety to choose from capable of running the most popular and capable OSes and applications.

#10529. Outback Steakhouse store closures: See a list of doomed locations as franchisee files for bankruptcy

A number of Outback Steakhouse locations closed their doors last month in the lead-up to a bankruptcy petition by one of the casual dining chain’s largest franchisees, court documents reveal. The store closures span four states. Here’s what to know.

What’s happened?

Cerca Trova Restaurant Group Holdings, which operates as Out West Restaurant Group, one of Outback Steakhouse’s largest franchisees, sought Chapter 11 bankruptcy protection in the United States Bankruptcy Court for the District of Delaware on Monday.

The San Diego-based company, which currently employs around 3,669 workers, operates 61 Outback Steakhouse restaurants across Arizona, California, Colorado, Nevada, and New Mexico.

Outback Steakhouse, the dining chain known for its Australian theme, had more than 660 U.S. restaurants as of the end of last year, according to parent company Bloomin’ Brands.

Why did Cerca Trova file for bankruptcy?

Court records show the franchisee filed for bankruptcy to sell the majority of its assets.

However, that same day, Cerca Trova filed a motion to reject the leases on 10 restaurant locations that it had closed between October 11 and October 25.

According to court documents, the shuttered restaurants operated at a loss or at margins insufficient to cover their occupancy costs. These locations aren’t part of the proposed sale. 

Which Outback Steakhouse locations recently closed?

The following Outback Steakhouse locations closed in October.

Arizona

  • 4871 E. Grant Road, Tucson
  • 1860 E. McKellips Road, Mesa

California

  • 7575 Beach Blvd., Buena Park
  • 25261 N. The Old Road, Valencia
  • 26652 Portola Parkway, Foothill Ranch

Colorado

  • 7065 Commerce Center Drive, Colorado Springs
  • 15 W. Springer Drive, Highlands Ranch
  • 2066 S. Abilene St., Aurora
  • 8601 W. Cross Drive, Littleton

Nevada

  • 3645 S. Virginia St., Reno

The franchisee had previously closed three underperforming locations earlier this year, court documents show.

Growing financial pressure since 2018

In court documents, the company noted that it has faced growing financial challenges since 2018 due to declining traffic and rising labor costs.

In 2020, during the COVID-19 pandemic, its revenue dropped around 35%. Cerca Trova has pursued a sale four times since 2018.

The company cited declining traffic and earnings—along with rising labor, food, and production costs—as the drivers of the mounting financial pressures that led to its recent bankruptcy filing.

On November 1, Bloomin’ Brands entered into a purchase agreement to acquire all of Cerca Trova’s assets for $26.3 million, subject to competing higher offers. The majority of Outback Steakhouse locations are already company-owned.

Fast Company reached out to Bloomin’ Brands to ask whether it plans to reopen any of the recently closed locations. We’ll update the story if we receive a reply.

#10526. Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi: Midterms sent a ‘very clear message’

Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said this morning that Democrats’ sweeping midterm victory sent a “very clear message” about the damage inflation has done to American consumers.  

During an appearance on CNBC’s Squawk Box, Khosrowshahi said the problem stems from how the economy has evolved since the 2008 financial crisis, as wages have not kept pace with skyrocketing prices.

“When you look at capitalism, there’s capital investment and return on capital, and obviously there’s return on labor,” he said. “If you look over the past 20 years, return on capital has increased very, very significantly. You can’t say the same thing about return on labor.”

The rise of artificial intelligence is only adding to workers’ anxiety, he added.

“AI is an instantiation of capital where, to some extent, capital could replace labor as well, which is rightfully, in some cases, scaring people,” Khosrowshahi said. “But it’s also very, very powerful in its potential.”

Khosrowshahi said he was sharing his opinion and that he is “not a politician.”

When asked how politicians and business leaders should respond, Khosrowshahi pointed to the tax code.

“[The fact that] capital gains are taxed at a lower rate than regular income makes no sense to me,” Khosrowshahi said. “They should be balanced.”

“Whether you should raise one or lower the other one, that’s really up to the folks in power,” he added. “But it doesn’t seem right to me.”

Khosrowshahi has led Uber since 2017, when he replaced cofounder Travis Kalanick amid a series of scandals involving the company’s workplace culture and leadership. Khosrowshahi was previously the CEO of online travel company Expedia.

Uber employs millions of drivers and couriers who work as independent contractors.

Khosrowshahi’s comments came on the same day Uber reported $14.8 billion in third-quarter revenue, up 10% from a year earlier, and $1.4 billion in operating income, up 30%.

The company also said it expects to have about 700 fully driverless vehicles operating on its platform by year-end.

#10525. Google Photos update fixes the bug that hid edited pictures

A bug in Google Photos has left edited pictures invisible to other Android apps, but Google has now rolled out a fix.

Since roughly July/August of this year, editing a picture in Google Photos has left Android users with the bizarre side effect of making that image unavailable to other apps. After saving the edit, the picture would vanish from the image picker in apps like Telegram, WhatsApp, and more. A workaround to this was to save the image as a copy rather than the original, but it’s frustrating nonetheless.

Google has thankfully, finally fixed this issue.

The fix is apparently in Google Photos v7.97, Artem Russakovskii (owner of APKMirror) mentions, and we’ve been able to confirm the hidden image behavior no longer occurs on v7.98 either. The company acknowledged the problem last month and confirmed a fix would be coming.

The exact cause remains unclear at this point, but that doesn’t matter now seeing as the problem is fixed. If you’re still seeing the bug, let us know in the comments below.

#10523. Apple is restricting a fast-growing category of apps. Here’s what users need to know

Apple is about to put greater restrictions on dating apps and AI companions. 

Starting on November 16, the company will require developers to declare whether their apps use AI to facilitate romantic connections. The apps that do use artificial intelligence—whether it’s an AI companion or technology that assists humans in connecting with one another—will only be allowed for users older than 18. 

According to Apple’s November 2 announcement, apps will have to declare whether they offer real-world location sharing, as well as “features that enable dating or relationship connections between real people and/or a virtual companion that engages a user in sexual or romantic content.”

In addition, the announcement stated that app creators “must provide these declarations when submitting an app update or making changes to your age-rating questionnaire.” It noted that the declarations must be complete by January 12, and said that all apps using the technology must have a minimum age rating of 18-plus. 

In some places, location sharing won’t automatically impact minimum age restrictions, such as in Brazil, where regulations only require an above-16 rating. 

Dating apps have been widely adopting AI to assist romance-seekers in making connections. Apps like Hinge, Tinder, and Bumble use AI for tasks like helping with profile creation, choosing photos, suggesting matches, and more. And earlier this year, Bumble announced it’s introducing an AI matchmaker named “Bee” to the app.

Of course, the age-related changes may not be widely felt on dating apps themselves, given most dating platforms already have 18-plus age restrictions in place. Still, many AI companion companies have a large number of teen users. Some of the most popular apps teenagers are using to connect with nonhuman companions are Character.AI, Nomi, Replika, and ChatGPT. But while ChatGPT and Claude aren’t aimed at companionship, teens are using them that way in droves. 

According to a 2025 survey from Common Sense Media, 72% of teens ages 13 to 17 have used AI companions at least once. But a staggering 52% engage with them regularly. In maybe the survey’s most telling finding, 31% said these interactions are more satisfying than talking to humans. 

Common Sense Media, a nonprofit that helps parents navigate tech and entertainment, has routinely recommended that AI companions should not be used by anyone younger than 18. In an April 2025 press release, James P. Steyer, the organization’s CEO, warned that AI companions are dangerous for minors for a host of reasons. “Social AI companions are not safe for kids. They are designed to create emotional attachment and dependency, which is particularly concerning for developing adolescent brains.”

Steyer continued: “Our testing showed these systems easily produce harmful responses, including sexual misconduct, stereotypes, and dangerous ‘advice’ that, if followed, could have life-threatening or deadly real-world impact for teens and other vulnerable people.” 

Fast Company reached out to Apple about the recent announcement but did not hear back by the time of publication.

Creality’s K3 is a solid entry into the swelling tool changer market, but without the lid and TPU Kit ready at launch, we’re left wondering what else this machine is capable of doing. The overly large spool holders impose a frustrating limit on the brands of filament you can use. Still, this is a good printer for fans of the Creality lineup who only need PLA or PETG.

Top hat and TPU printing kit not available at launch

Spool holders are too large for many 3rd party spools

Why you can trust Tom's Hardware Our expert reviewers spend hours testing and comparing products and services so you can choose the best for you. Find out more about how we test.

Creality has finally caught up with the tool changer fad, presenting us with a speedy, four-nozzle system named “KliTek” mounted on a Creality K3. Tool changers are the way to go, since they do not compromise speed for color and eliminate the need to waste your filament in the form of “printer poop.” The K3 is still programmed to create a purge tower on multicolor prints, but this is a small fraction of the filament wasted using any type of AMS-style color system.

The new KliTek nozzle system supports printing with different-sized nozzles in the same print, which sounds more useful than I actually found practical. Users will also be able to blend colors in Creality Print, a trick picked up from Snapmaker’s open-source Full Spectrum. This method creates the optical illusion of new colors by stacking very thin layers of filament.

The tool-changing system works very well and never dropped or misplaced a tool during the review. Creality has tucked 37 sensors inside the printer, with 12 dedicated to the nozzle swapping process alone. No, I’m not going to name all of them, but they do work. I didn’t get a single bad print during the review, even when running at higher speeds.

However, the K3 looks suspiciously like a Snapmaker U1 clone, departing from the black and grey aesthetic of the K1 and K2 3D printers. It has conveniently placed, side-mounted spool holders that are a tad too large for many 3rd party brands of filament. We’re not sure if they’re trying to herd us towards a walled garden of Creality plastics, or if they simply didn’t check out all the options.

Unfortunately, the Creality K3 needs a lid for printing high-temperature filaments, and this “tophat” was not ready at the time of the review. Creality says the top hat will be packaged with a TPU Kit to enable the printing of super soft materials.

The K3 is currently on preorder with a price tag of $849. The competition for affordable tool changers is pretty stiff, and Creality hasn’t brought anything new to the table, which is keeping the K3 off our list of the very best 3D printers you can buy. But if you’re a fan of the Creality ecosystem, it’s a welcome addition to the fleet.

PLA/PETG/PCTG/TPU/CF and GF filled (up to 300 °C)

Double-sided Textured PEI steel flex plate (up to 100 °C)

482 x 420 x 536 mm (18.97 x 16.53 x 21.10 in)

The Creality K3 comes with everything you need to assemble and maintain your printer. The included tool kit has hex keys, side cutters, grease, and a nice nozzle cleaner. There is also a paper copy of the quick installation guide and a 200g spool of white Creality filament.

Get Tom's Hardware's best news and in-depth reviews, straight to your inbox.

The Creality K3 has four tools, each with a built-in ceramic heater, nozzle with a hardened steel insert, and filament path. The KliTek system supports printing with different nozzle sizes and different materials in the same print. Like the Prusa/Bondtech INDX, the extruder and cooling fan are mounted on a single toolhead.

The rest of the Creality K3 shares its design with the K2. The printer has a solid metal frame clad in white plastic and a glass door with dampened hinges. The motion system is Core XY, with a linear rail for the X axis and linear rods for the Y axis. The bed rides on four linear rods driven by 2 lead screws belted to a single stepper motor on the bottom of the printer. Parts cooling is provided by a blower fan in the toolhead and a large side-mounted blower fan mounted on the left side of the case. The stock Creality K3 comes with an open top, so chamber cooling is not an issue. Unfortunately, this makes the printer rather loud.

The Creality K3 has a 720p camera located at the top right of the printer, which does a great job providing print monitoring from the device tab in the slicer and the Creality Cloud app. There is also an AI camera that monitors for build plate detection, foreign object detection, and spaghetti detection. There were no false positives during the test.

We did not get to review the special TPU kit, which will allow the machine to run super soft TPU, which is becoming quite trendy for those interested in printing shoes. The kit will replace the CFS Nano material handler with a CFS Flex and add dry boxes for the filament and a special high-flow nozzle. The kit will be bundled with a lid/ tophat with ventilation and air filtration.

The Creality K3 arrives with some assembly required. After removing the packing material, you need to remove the four screws securing the bed for shipping, and there is a nice reminder to do this when first firing up the printer.

The spool holders twist into the printer’s side panels and are numbered to match the filament slots. Two PTFE guide brackets, also numbered, need to be secured to the rear of the printer with M4x6 screws, as does the bracket for the CFS Nano. There is a communication cable that runs from the rear of the printer to the CFS Nano as well.

The tool cables attach to the top of the printer with 2 M4x12 screws each, with the PTFE tubes running to the CFS Nano. The toolhead communication cable is attached with M3x5 screws on the toolhead and M4x8 screws on the right side of the printer. Attaching PTFE guide tubes from the side brackets up to the CFS Nano completes the assembly.

The Creality K3 does an excellent job calibrating and bed leveling as part of its initial self-check. Bed leveling can be repeated at the start of each print.

Loading filament into the Creality K3 is pretty simple. Filament is inserted into a port on the side bracket, which guides it up to the CFS Nano, which does the rest. The filament waits in the tube until called for by a print job. It is then loaded into the tool.

To unload, the tool is selected from the printer’s screen. The printer then cuts the filament and retracts it out of the tool, and it can be manually pulled out of the CFS Nano the rest of the way.

All four filament slots can read RFID tags in the spools to load information for Creality-branded filament. For other filament brands, the printer will beep to remind you to manually enter the filament type and color.

The latest version of Creality Print 7.3 is available from Creality.com. It is based on the Orca Slicer and Ultimaker Cura Engine. The default settings worked well, and there is a new AI assistant mode, which is still labeled as beta. At the time of the review, the only thing missing for the K3 was a button to map the filaments into the slicer. The button is still there for the earlier K-series printers in the slicer. The slicer does have filament mixing for more color combinations.

A link at the top of the page will take you to Creality’s AI Creation tools and Creality Cloud, Creality’s online file-sharing service. If you don’t like the Cloud, you can export files from the slicer and either move them to the printer with a USB stick or move them over your home network by accessing the printer’s FLUIDD interface. To access FLUIDD, you need to find the IP address of your printer and type that into a browser window, followed by:4408 with no spaces.

The Creality K3 comes with a 200g spool of white Hyper PLA. If you want more colors and materials, you should check out our guide to the best filaments for 3D printing for suggestions.

For the first print, I was going to run a pumpkin fidget toy, so I grabbed a spool of Prusa orange and was really quite cross when it didn’t fit on the preposterously large spool holders. I decided right then to mod the spool holder with the Creality Pika scanner. I took the scan into Tinkercad and reduced the diameter of the spool holder, then ran the new spool holders in Inland basic white using a .2 layer height and an average print speed of 170mm/s. The print took 8 hours and 34 minutes to complete. I do not usually mod printers while reviewing them, but Prusa Orange is perfect for pumpkins.

Below is the original spool holder (left) and the modded version (right).

For my second print, I did a pumpkin fidget toy I found on MakerWorld using Prusa orange PLA, Elegoo green PLA Pro, and Polymaker black HT-PLA Pro. I used a .2 mm layer height and printed with an average speed of 160mm/s; the print took a little over six hours. It came out nice without a hint of overextrusion. I liked it so much I decided to print it again scaled up to 200%. Using the same settings, the larger print took 16 hours and 28 minutes and is also very nice with a good fidget action.

For PETG, I printed a plate of 3 flexy geckos I found on Creality Cloud using Prusa Carmine Red, Prusa Sky Blue, and Bambu Lab basic white PETG. Using a .2mm layer height and running at 180mm/s, the print took 5 hours 45 minutes to complete. The geckos are smooth and clean, plus all of the links work perfectly with no stringing or overextrusion present.

The Creality K3 did not have its special “flex” CFS at the time of review, but I decided to try TPU anyway. I printed some omni wheels for a Death Racer we’re working on in both hard TPU for MFS from Inland and some 95A Inland rainbow TPU. The stock CFS Nano had no trouble pushing these, and the toolhead extruder had no problem with it. It did well. Trouble came when I tried some 90A TPU from Bambu Lab. I’d stick to the harder stuff until the TPU kit is ready.

I did get good prints with the black TPU for AMS and the rainbow 95A filaments. The prints are omni-wheel rollers from the Deathracer project of Michael Baddeley. Both sets of eight rollers were printed at a .2mm layer height at an average speed of 50mm/s and each took a little over 4 hours to print. There was a tiny bit of stringing, but otherwise the rollers are perfect.

The Creality K3 is a terrific printer that should become more capable with accessories like the tophat and TPU kit in the future. The oversized spools are a little annoying, but easily fixed. The only thing I worry about is Creality’s track record of releasing a printer, then introducing a better “pro” or “max” model within four months. I wouldn’t be surprised if we get a six- or eight-color K3 variant before next spring.

At its prelaunch price of $849, it’s $100 more than a similarly equipped, slightly larger Snapmaker U1, which is a tough place to be. It is also the same price as the fully enclosed Flashforge Creator 5 Pro, which we didn’t review, but we did check out the budget model Flashforge Creator 5, which is currently available for $699.

MORE: Best Budget 3D Printers for Beginners

Denise Bertacchi is a Contributing Writer for Tom’s Hardware US, covering 3D printing. Denise has been crafting with PCs since she discovered Print Shop had clip art on her Apple IIe. She loves reviewing 3D printers because she can mix all her passions: printing, photography, and writing.

#10520. Elon Musk spent nearly $500 million on the midterms. It bought him almost nothing

Elon Musk put about $474 million into the 2026 midterms, according to a New York Times tally. (That amount only tracks through October 14, when Federal Election Commission [FEC] and IRS filings stopped; the trillionaire may have given far more in dark money.) For comparison, the world’s richest man spent an estimated $250 million to get Donald Trump elected in 2024.

But this time, he has little to show for his efforts. Democrats wrested control of both the House of Representatives and Senate from Republicans Tuesday night. A Forbes analysis shows that 44 of Musk’s 106 candidates lost, including in the races that mattered most to him: Ken Paxton’s bid for a Texas Senate seat, Greg Abbott’s bid to remain Texas governor, and Vivek Ramaswamy’s bid for governor of Ohio. Eighteen Musk-backed candidates won, but all were in seats Republicans were expected to win anyway. Another 44 races remained uncalled Wednesday.

Musk’s money was funneled to Republican House and Senate candidates through his own super PAC, America PAC (about $216 million), the Senate Leadership Fund ($168 million), and the Congressional Leadership Fund for House races ($30 million).

The largest share of Musk’s midterm spending ($212 million) went toward helping Ken Paxton beat James Talarico for the Texas Senate seat formerly held by John Cornyn. Talarico walloped Paxton Tuesday night, winning by 12 points in the traditionally red state. In his victory speech, Talarico seemed to call out Musk, saying he had sent “a message to every billionaire megadonor, every trillionaire megadonor.”

Outside Texas, America PAC spent $22.7 million in six battleground states through October 20, filings show, including $8.9 million in Ohio and $7.2 million in Michigan. Democrat Sherrod Brown won the Senate seat in Ohio, while Abdul El-Sayed won the Senate seat in Michigan.

Congressional purse strings

Musk’s America PAC said its “only priority is ensuring Republicans keep full control of Washington.” His businesses rely heavily on federal money: SpaceX booked $6.78 billion in federal contracts through October 1, compared with just $3.8 billion in all of 2024, per data from federal spending tracker FedScout. In May, the U.S. Space Force awarded it $4.16 billion for Golden Dome tracking satellites. The party that controls Congress controls the government’s purse strings. Musk’s gravy train may slow down or stop.

Republicans believed Democrats would have to take Texas to seize control of Congress.

In January, Democrats will chair the committees that fund and oversee SpaceX’s biggest customers. Sen. Susan Collins (R-ME), whom America PAC backed, lost her seat—and with it, the Appropriations Committee chairmanship, which shapes NASA and Pentagon budgets.

Sen. Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, the top Democrat on the Permanent Subcommittee on Investigations, has said he would investigate Musk and the Department of Government Efficiency (DOGE) if Democrats won. The Senate also confirms Federal Communications Commission (FCC) members, who control Starlink’s spectrum, and funds the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA), which licenses SpaceX launches. The new Congress can’t cancel contracts; the Pentagon and NASA award them.

With Paxton’s defeat, Musk also lost a reliable vote in the Senate—and gained a Texas senator in Talarico who identified him during the campaign as an out-of-touch trillionaire who personifies some of the country’s biggest problems.

Investigations

As Democrats clinched the House on Tuesday night, Rep. Robert Garcia (D-CA), who will chair the House Oversight Committee, posted two words on X: “LAWYER UP.” The warning was aimed mainly at the Trump administration and family, but Garcia’s office said he would also take on “corporate corruption,” and Musk may be at the top of that list. Democrats will run committees with subpoena power, allowing them to compel documents and testimony. In 2025, House Republicans blocked a Democratic motion to subpoena Musk. In January, Democrats will hold the gavels.

They’ve already named their targets. Committees are weighing probes of Musk’s time running DOGE, SpaceX’s and Tesla’s federal contracts, and his alleged role in restricting SpaceX’s Starshield satellite service to Ukraine’s military, Politico reports. (Musk says the U.S. military, not SpaceX, decides any limits on Starshield.)

Wall Street investors reacted quickly to Tuesday night’s election results. SpaceX shares fell 3.8% and Tesla dropped 3.5% in premarket trading on Wednesday. Overnight, Musk posted on X: “Data centers in space looking pretty appealing right now.”

What Hinojosa’s win means in Texas

Democrat Gina Hinojosa’s surprise victory over Gov. Greg Abbott could put Musk’s plans to build data centers across Texas in jeopardy. Hinojosa has proposed a moratorium on new data center construction until lawmakers enact lasting safeguards. “Data centers are coming in and doing as they please—they are guzzling up all our water, guzzling up all our electricity—and the people have no say . . . that is the Wild West of data centers that Greg Abbott has created in Texas,” she said in July.

Hinojosa wants rules giving Texas residents more say over new developments, requiring companies to prove their projects won’t raise household water or electricity bills, and prohibiting nondisclosure agreements that keep communities in the dark during the permitting process. She also wants to eliminate the government subsidies that have helped make Texas so attractive to developers.

Musk has major operations and investments in the state, including Tesla’s headquarters and largest U.S. plant, SpaceX’s Starbase launch site, and the planned Terafab semiconductor and AI chip plant. Musk gave an estimated $5.5 million to Abbott’s campaign.

Abbott’s administration gave Musk’s companies some major benefits. The governor’s office pushed broadband rules that favored Starlink, which then won about $110 million in state grants, triggering an audit. Terafab won about $1.7 billion in school tax breaks, and SpaceX more than $54 million in state grants, according to a lawsuit Hinojosa filed during the campaign.

That suit won Hinojosa access to more than 1,000 pages of Abbott-Musk communications that Abbott had called too “intimate and embarrassing” to release. In one message, Musk asked whether Abbott would “have his back,” to which Abbott replied, “100%.”

When she takes office in January, Hinojosa will control future incentive deals. She’ll also appoint the Texas Parks commissioners who would vote on any sale of Boca Chica State Park, which Musk wants to buy to expand SpaceX’s Starbase rocket facility in South Texas.

What the losses cost Musk

The $224 million Musk spent and lost in Texas isn’t likely to hurt his wallet much. He’s worth about $902 billion today, so he lost roughly one-fortieth of 1% of his wealth.

But the loss of a friendly Congress—and the diminished political clout of Musk’s friend Trump—could cost much more. About one-fifth of SpaceX’s $18.7 billion in 2025 revenue came from federal agencies, its initial public offering (IPO) filing says. That’s roughly $3.7 billion a year, or $7.5 billion over two years at 2025 levels. The Democratic Congress could decide to slow-walk new contracts, like May’s $4.16 billion Golden Dome award.

Musk now pitches SpaceX as a supplier of AI computing. Deals renting its Colossus data centers to Anthropic and Google could bring in $26 billion a year. The changing political tide could make getting permits for new data centers more difficult. In August, even the Musk-friendly Abbott paused new data center connections to the Texas grid.

The election results could also shake investors’ confidence in Musk and the companies he leads. SpaceX’s IPO filing calls the company “highly dependent” on Musk. When investors buy SpaceX or Tesla stock, they’re not just looking at the companies’ financials; they’re also buying into the “story” of Musk, who has fashioned an image of an unpredictable engineering genius with massive wealth and powerful friends. But his political connections look considerably less secure after Tuesday night. That could make investors less inclined to believe Musk’s claims that SpaceX will put data centers in space and become the largest AI company in the world.

On Tuesday morning, Musk tweeted “Vote red today!” But by Wednesday morning, the tweet had quietly disappeared.

#10519. Samsung just released a new foldable that you probably wouldn’t buy even if you could

Samsung has big plans for its foldable lineup in 2027, but also one more release for 2026. The Galaxy W27 just went official as the company’s latest foldable, but you probably wouldn’t want to buy this one even if you could.

The Galaxy W27 continues Samsung’s pattern of releasing a China-exclusive variant of its flagship, book-style foldable. This year, it’s based on the Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra and includes all of the same specs – 8-inch inner display, Snapdragon 8 Elite Gen 5, 200MP main camera, and everything else.

It mostly comes down to the fit and finish. Samsung has given the Galaxy W27 some slick golden accents and two striking color variants. One is a dark red, the other a dark blue. This model also comes with 16GB of RAM as standard, regardless of if you pick the 512GB or 1TB storage options. It’s also optimized for Tiantong satellite comms, SamMobile points out.

But this special edition comes at a cost. It starts at CNY 18,999, around $2,800 USD. The 1TB upgrade lands at CNY 21,999, around $3,300 USD. So, even if you could buy this model, you’d likely be better off going with the standard Galaxy Z Fold 8 Ultra – even the maxed-out 1TB model sells for less at $2,699. Samsung does include a case and even a charging brick in the box with the Galaxy W27, though.

#10518. Canva’s big layoffs say a lot about the AI design landscape

The AI design giant Canva just announced the first-ever major round of layoffs in its 13-year history. As part of the restructuring, 1,271 people—around 22% of the company’s overall staff—will either be laid off, reassigned to new roles, or relocated to the company’s headquarters in Sydney, Australia. 

News of the layoffs was announced on November 3 (a perfect day to bury some bad news) in a press release from Canva cofounder and CEO Melanie Perkins. In the note, Perkins explains that the layoffs are part of a larger plan to make Canva’s teams more agile and less siloed, including by folding product, growth, and platform teams into one unit and reducing the number of “subspecialities” at the company.

“I’ve come to the difficult conclusion that small changes won’t be enough,” Perkins’ letter reads. “To set ourselves up for the next decade, we need to refound Canva, getting back to our roots of small, empowered teams with the freedom to make decisions, take ownership, and focus on what matters most for our community.”

While Canva didn’t provide a broader business reason for the layoffs, the restructuring comes at a time when it’s working through some mounting growing pains and questions about the timing of a potential initial public offering (IPO). After spending the last several years going all in on its AI-powered product suite, Canva is now facing the challenge of squaring its business model with an increasingly voracious user base.

Canva’s growth conundrum

In May, Fast Company wrote that design was entering its “frenemies” era. 

At the time, Anthropic had just launched Claude Design. The product seemingly came as a surprise to incumbent companies including Adobe and Figma, which had been operating under a multiyear collaboration with Anthropic to integrate Claude into their products, and didn’t expect the AI giant to debut its own design competitor. Meanwhile, Canva told Fast Company that it had actually helped Anthropic develop Claude Design, despite Canva’s own collaboration deal with the company. 

For Adobe, Figma, and Canva, working with frontier models offers the advantage of bringing new tools to market faster and benefiting from the sophistication of frontier models. The main downside is that using these frontier models also takes a lot of computing power, and that racks up major costs. As Canva has made a major push—by building its own models and acquiring AI companies—to become an “AI platform” over the last several years, those costs have become a significant problem.

In early August, Canva sent a note to its investors with an update: The company was downgrading its revenue growth forecast for 2026 from 30% to 20%. At the time, Perkins told shareholders that the “average cost of serving an AI task was too high” as the company relied heavily on its partnerships with frontier models to complete users’ requests. 

For context, by the end of 2025, Canva had more than 265 million monthly active users and more than 31 million paid users, meaning that some large portion of AI traffic on the site was likely generated by free users. In an August interview with Fortune, Perkins said that users’ demand for new AI features had “significantly exceeded” the company’s expectations, which came with both pros and cons. 

“This validated the demand, but also showed us we needed to reduce the cost of completing an AI task to support a broad rollout,” Perkins told the publication. “Rather than broadly rolling out a product before the underlying economics were ready, we decided to slow the rollout while we rebuilt the architecture, reduced unit costs, and strengthened the business model.”

To reduce the intermediary costs that Canva incurs every time an AI task requires a frontier model, Canva has been working on developing first-party tools that can take up some of the work. For example, Perkins told Fortune that, since launching Canva 2.0 in April, the company’s cost-per-task has reduced by 90%. This October, Canva launched another product called Canva Brush, which it said reduced cost-per-task by 46% compared with the previous design agent. 

These new features have made improvements, but, based on its downgraded revenue forecast, Canva still has a ways to go before it fully irons out its economic model. The fact that user demand for Canva’s AI tools is outpacing its own capabilities seems to be a bullish sign for AI design at large. Now, Canva needs to figure out how to make the most of the surge—and the company’s first major layoffs could be part of its plan to get back on track.
